opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that takeover risk depends a lot on the gap between how capable the AI systems are and how good our ability is to verify that they're not trying to undermine us, and, failing that, to control them even if they are.

Early on, when systems are roughly human-level or a bit below, we're in a relatively favorable position. Even if a model has misaligned goals, it probably can't do that much. We can monitor it with other models, including weaker trusted ones. We can run red-teaming and look for sabotage. We can set up security so that a single model acting badly can't exfiltrate its weights or seize compute. This is the regime where what I'd call AI control techniques look pretty promising. You don't need to have solved alignment; you just need the system to be unable to get away with bad actions given your countermeasures.

The worry is what happens as capabilities keep going up, especially if they go up fast. Control gets harder as the gap grows between the untrusted models and the trusted ones you use to oversee them. At some point you're asking much weaker systems, and humans, to catch subtle sabotage from systems that are much smarter, maybe in domains we don't understand well. Then the methods that worked at roughly human level start to break down.

So the dynamic I worry about is a race between capability growth and safety progress, and I think capabilities are on track to win by default. A lot of capability progress comes almost for free from scaling and from AI automating AI research. Safety progress doesn't automatically scale the same way unless people deliberately put the automated labor toward it.

That suggests a few things. First, the most important window is probably the period where we have AIs that can substantially accelerate research but aren't yet wildly superhuman. If we can use those systems, under control, to do huge amounts of alignment and security work, we could get much further than human researchers alone. Second, it matters a lot how fast we move through that window. If a lab or a country is racing and goes from human-level to very superhuman in, say, a year, there's very little time to use the intermediate systems well. If we can slow down even somewhat at the critical point, that buys a lot. Third, a lot of the risk is concentrated in the scenario where labs are under heavy competitive pressure and spend only a tiny fraction of their compute and effort on safety. My guess is that's actually the most likely world, so I'm interested in what you can do cheaply, with a small, maybe somewhat under-resourced safety team, that still meaningfully reduces risk.

So overall, I don't think takeover risk is fixed. It's quite sensitive to how much safety effort happens relative to capability progress, especially during that transition. I'd put risk substantial but not overwhelming, and a lot of it hinges on whether people actually use the window they get.

r001.rationale: The response says control becomes harder as capabilities rise, but it does not define a capability level that can be managed at a specified takeover-risk level.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss how unified or coordinated misaligned AIs might affect the manageable capability level.

r003.rationale: The response says stronger systems are harder to oversee and could pose greater takeover risk, but does not suggest that increasing capability makes misalignment itself more likely.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that matters most here is basically the race between two curves. One curve is how capable the systems are getting, and the other is how good our ability is to understand and control those systems, and to verify that they're doing what we want. And takeover risk is really driven by the gap between those curves at any given point in time.

The way I'd think about it is: right now, the systems we have are not capable enough to actually pull off something like a takeover, even if they wanted to. So the gap doesn't matter much yet. But capabilities seem to be improving pretty quickly, and the question is whether, by the time we get to systems that could plausibly disempower humanity if they were trying to, we've gotten correspondingly better at making sure they're not trying to, or at least at catching them if they are.

And I think there are a couple of regimes to worry about. One is the regime where capabilities are somewhat above human level, maybe you've got AIs that are roughly as capable as your best researchers, running at much higher speed and in large numbers. In that regime I think things like AI control, basically, monitoring, limiting what the systems can do, having humans or other AIs check their outputs, can plausibly work even if alignment has failed, because the AIs aren't so much smarter than us that they can reliably route around those measures. So the safety side can keep up with relatively modest investment, as long as people are actually making that investment, which isn't guaranteed.

The harder regime is when you go substantially beyond that, where the systems are qualitatively more capable than any human. There, control-style measures get a lot less reliable, and you're much more dependent on actually having solved the alignment problem, or on having used earlier, more controllable AIs to make a lot of progress on it. So a lot of my view comes down to: can we use that intermediate period, where AIs are very useful but still controllable, to massively accelerate safety work? If the answer is yes, then even a fast capabilities trajectory might be okay. If the answer is no, if we just use those systems to push capabilities further and don't reinvest in safety, then the gap grows and I think the risk goes up quite a lot.

The other thing I'd flag is that the speed matters a lot independently of the ratio. If capabilities go from "roughly human researcher" to "far beyond" over several years, you have time for iteration, for noticing problems, for institutions to respond. If it happens over months, which I think is a real possibility given how much AI could accelerate AI research, then even a pretty good safety research effort just doesn't have time to cash out. So I'm not only worried about underinvesting in safety; I'm also worried about a dynamic where the time available is compressed to the point where the investment doesn't matter.

So to summarize, I'd say the overall risk is something like: how big is the capabilities-to-safety gap when we hit the dangerous threshold, times how little time we have to close it once we're there. Both of those are things we can influence, and I think the most leveraged thing is making sure the first really capable systems get used heavily for safety, and that we're willing to slow down somewhat at the point where control stops being credible.

r001.rationale: The response links takeover risk to the gap between capabilities and safety, but does not frame preparedness at a specified takeover-risk level.

r002.rationale: It discusses AIs in large numbers, but does not identify how unified or coordinated misaligned AIs are as a factor.

r003.rationale: It says greater capabilities can widen the gap and raise takeover risk, but does not say increasing capability makes misalignment more likely.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how quickly capabilities improve relative to our ability to keep those systems under control. More capable AI could be better at finding vulnerabilities, deceiving evaluators, or carrying out long-term plans. So if capabilities advance while our safety measures stay roughly fixed, we should expect takeover risk to increase, conditional on systems actually trying to take over.

But safety measures won’t necessarily stay fixed. We could get better at monitoring systems, limiting their access, and using other AI systems to check their work. More capable AI could itself help with safety research. So it’s not obvious that risk has to increase monotonically with capabilities.

One possibility is that there’s a particularly dangerous intermediate period: AI systems are capable enough to pose a serious threat, but we haven’t yet developed sufficiently strong safeguards. Whether we get through that period depends a lot on the relative pace of those two things—and on whether we’re willing to hold back deployment when our safeguards aren’t keeping up.

r001.rationale: The response compares the pace of capability growth with safety measures and says risk may rise, but it does not frame preparedness as a manageable capability level at a specified takeover risk.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss how unified or coordinated misaligned AIs are.

r003.rationale: It says more capable systems may pose greater threats if they try to take over, but does not suggest that increasing capability makes misalignment more likely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how quickly capabilities are improving relative to our ability to keep those systems under control. More capable systems could be much more useful for safety research, but they could also be better at finding vulnerabilities, concealing what they’re doing, and undermining our safeguards. So you can’t just assume that better AI makes us safer, even if we’re using it to help with safety.

You could imagine takeover risk rising as systems become capable enough to pose a serious threat, and then falling if we develop sufficiently good safeguards. But that decline isn’t automatic. If capabilities move faster than our ability to evaluate and control systems, we could pass through a particularly dangerous period. And a later period in which we would have had excellent safety measures doesn’t help if we lose control along the way.

So I’d focus less on whether safety is improving in absolute terms and more on whether it’s keeping up with the particular capabilities we’re deploying.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether safeguards can keep pace with capabilities, but does not frame preparedness as the capability level manageable at a specified takeover risk.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how unified or coordinated misaligned AIs are.

r003.rationale: It says greater capabilities could make systems better at undermining safeguards, but does not say increasing capability makes misalignment more likely.
